items.title: From Hijacked PBX to Stolen Trunk: INJ3CTOR3’s Campaign Evolves
items.summary: Executive Summary In May, Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) documented JOMANGY , a PHP webshell generation deployed by INJ3CTOR3 with self-healing persistence channels and a built-in toll-fraud dialer. Back then, the fraud ran through the victim's own PBX, so removing the implant would have stopped it. Artifacts we collected from the operator's C2 staging servers during mid-September 2026 show that this is no longer true: the installer now sends credentials off the box on every run, and a second staging host serves it. INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now uploads the victim's SIP trunk, AMI, database, and mail-relay credentials to the operator, so disinfecting or rebuilding an infected host no longer ends the exposure. Anyone running FreePBX, Issabel, or Elastix who suspects compromise must rotate the secrets in 17 configuration files, and only after the host is clean. The infection and persistence code is nearly unchanged; what the operator rotated are the identifiers that were available to defenders since the last time. Each section below pairs a finding with what to do about it. Key Takeaways Credentials leave on every run. k.php uploads 17 configuration files to both staging hosts every minute the host stays infected. The fraud no longer needs your PBX. A stolen trunk secret lets the operator register and place calls as you from anywhere. Last report's identifiers have expired. Each build now carries its own watermark, and the webshell gate hash was rotated. Two staging hosts. Plain-text commands now point to 160[.]119[.]69[.]4, while base64-encoded ones still use 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. Clean-looking logs and consoles prove nothing. Requests through an encoded space reach the shell without being named in the access log, and trunks are written directly to /etc/asterisk; they do not appear in the FreePBX console. The Campaign So Far INJ3CTOR3 has been abusing Asterisk-based phone systems for toll fraud since at least 2020. Check Point Research named the operation that November, when it exploited CVE-2019-19006 in FreePBX and used a basic webshell to read amportal.conf and sip_additional.conf by hand. Unit 42 reported a related operation against Elastix in 2022, Fortinet documented the EncystPHP webshell in January 2026, and our May report covered JOMANGY. The playbook has held for six years: scan for exposed PBXs, exploit or brute-force a way in, plant a password -gated webshell, and dial out at the victim's expense. Figure 1 below shows the chain as it stands in the September build, now including the credential upload back to the staging hosts. Figure 1: INJ3CTOR3 attack chain, September generation. (Source: 0x1da5 GitHub) What Changed Since Our Last Report We compared the April artifacts behind our May report with the 9 September collection from both staging hosts, after decoding every layer. Area April September Credential Exfiltration None 17 files to /hima_data/index.php on both hosts Staging hosts 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 and 160[.]119[.]69[.]4 webshell watermark One value in every copy A different value per build Webshell gate hash (JOMANGY and ZenharR) a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a /x takeover script 367 lines 620 lines, mostly added cleanup: removing rival actors’ implants and SSH keys wor.php, people2.txt, _*.php status files Present Absent from the collection Unchanged: the decoded webshell panel, the encoding chain (base64 in the shell script, base64 again in PHP, then ROT13), the persistence channels, the backdoor account password hash, and the borrowed timestamp. Behavioral detections built on our May report still apply. Credential Exfiltration: The Implant Is No Longer the Product The September k.php ends with two new base64-encoded lines, each holding 17 curl commands that upload one configuration file apiece to /hima_data/index.php, one line per staging host (See Figure 2 below). The paths are typed out by hand and cover FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix layouts. The collector path echoes hima, a backdoor account the takeover script creates. The name goes back further: Check Point's 2020 INJ3CTOR3 report shows a Telegram post by a user called Hima sharing a tool that scans and cracks SIP ranges, saving its output as HimaResults. Figure 2: k.php line 34, decoded into 17 file uploads Three of the cron beacons fetch and run k.php every minute (the others every two or three minutes), so the upload repeats every minute during the infection. Rotating credentials on a still-infected host hands the new secrets to the operator within minutes. What it unlocks Files uploaded Rotate SIP trunks and extensions (chan_sip) /etc/asterisk/sip.conf, sip_additional.conf, sip_registrations.conf, sip_general_additional.conf, sip_custom.conf Every trunk secret (with your carrier) and extension secret, changed in the FreePBX GUI, since the *_additional.conf files are regenerated SIP trunks and extensions (PJSIP) /etc/asterisk/pjsip.auth.conf, pjsip.endpoint.conf, pjsip.aor.conf, pjsip.identify.conf, pjsip.transports.conf The same secrets; review IP-based identity rules Call origination without SIP /etc/asterisk/manager.conf Every AMI user. PBX database, AMI, and platform admin /etc/freepbx.conf, /etc/amportal.conf, /etc/asterisk/amportal.conf, /etc/issabel.conf, /etc/elastix.conf The database password (AMPDBPASS), the MySQL root password, and any AMI password stored there Outbound mail /etc/postfix/sasl_passwd The SMTP relay account, with your mail provider This opens a second route to fraud. Our May report covered calls placed through the webshell, which require the shell to be alive and to land in the victim's own call records. With a stolen trunk secret, the operator can register to the carrier from any machine and call as the victim, leaving nothing on the host, unless the carrier also restricts the trunk to the victim's IP addresses. A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second. Detection Network: outbound HTTP POSTs from a PBX to any /hima_data/ path or to either staging host. A PBX seldom needs outbound web access beyond vendor updates, so egress allow-listing closes this channel. Carrier: alert on trunk registrations from outside your own IP ranges, and on premium or international destinations, off-hours calling, and unusual concurrency. Set spend caps and destination blocks where your carrier offers them. For Law Enforcement Agencies and CERTs By design, victims' credentials were collected on the two staging hosts, which stopped responding in late September 2026. Going offline does not end exposure: hosting providers may still retain server data, and infected PBXs keep trying to upload their credentials every minute to addresses that could be reassigned to someone else. Both are reasons for law enforcement and national CERTs, which have the legal standing that researchers lack, to work with the providers on preserving that data and sinkholing the addresses, which would also identify victims for notification. We saw the uploads in code; we did not capture one in transit and hold no victim list. Two Staging Hosts, Split by Encoding An infected host now talks to both staging hosts, and which one depends on whether the command was written in plain text or base64. The /x takeover script is byte-identical on both. Reference Encoding Points to k.php line 2 (re-runs /x), eight cron schedules in /x, wr.php's callback Plain text 160[.]119[.]69[.]4 Camouflaged cron payloads, login-triggered stager Base64 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 Credential upload Base64 Both In April, all of these pointed to 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. We assess that the operator replaced the address in plain text and never re-encoded the base64 strings; the credential upload, which names both hosts, appears deliberate. This host is distinct from the scanner 160[.]119[.]76[.]250, which is named in our May report. Defend: block both hosts in both directions, and decode every base64-encoded string in a crontab or shell profile before deciding which hosts a host talks to. A plain-text review would miss every channel that still reaches 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. The Webshell: Same Program, New Identifiers Decoded, the September JOMANGY panel is identical to April's except for the values defenders were told to look for. Per-build watermark. Our May report advised hunting for trace_e1ebf9066a951be519a24140711839ea, present in every April copy. The September builds carry trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 (45[.]95[.]147[.]178) and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e (160[.]119[.]69[.]4), so that hunt now misses current infections. One gate for two generations. JOMANGY and ZenharR share a single hardcoded MD5 gate hash, rotated together from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a. Our May report listed the April value under ZenharR only. A forged administrator session. Behind the gate, the FreePBX button builds an admin session using FreePBX's own ampuser class and setAdmin(); in our lab, it opened the full console without any password. Therefore, changing the FreePBX admin password affects neither the gate nor this session. (See Figure 3 below) Figure 3: The panel's Freepbx and Elastix buttons forge an admin session without a password Because each of these identifiers changes between builds, the detection approach later in this report focuses on who put a file on disk rather than on what the file contains. The .htaccess Door and the Access-Log Gap k.php writes a seven-line .htaccess to /var/www/html/admin/views/. It does not hide the webshell; it unblocks it, and it lets requests reach a copy without naming it. RewriteEngine On # enable symbolic links Options +FollowSymLinks RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-l RewriteRule ^\s+ config.php [L] Request path Status What answered /dir/zzz 404 Nothing /dir/%20zzz, /dir/%09zzz (space, tab, etc) 200 config.php /dir/+zzz 404 Nothing Simulating an operator and a victim in an isolated environment, we confirmed that a request to a URL containing an encoded space returned a working webshell for the attacker. The access log records only the requested path, never the file that answered, so searching logs for the webshell by its filename can return nothing on a host that is serving it . Defend: check every .htaccess across the web root for who put it there; one that no package, FreePBX module, or member of your team accounts for is suspect, whatever it contains. Because the takeover script wipes logs, treat log hunting as secondary: requests with %20, %09, or %0A directly after a slash that return 200 are worth a look where logs survive. What the FreePBX Console Won't Show You FreePBX lists the trunks it created from its own database; Asterisk reads whatever is in its configuration files. In our lab, a trunk we wrote directly into /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf carried a call while the FreePBX Trunks page reported no records (See Figure 4 below). We did not see the campaign plant one, but its root-equivalent accounts and stolen trunk secrets give the operator everything needed to do so. Figure 4: Our lab trunk, known to Asterisk and carrying calls, invisible in the FreePBX console Defend: audit from the Asterisk CLI (pjsip show endpoints, pjsip show registrations, sip show peers, sip show registry) and compare with what the console lists. Review the *_custom.conf files for trunks or contexts that nobody on your team added. What Keeps It There Before detecting or cleaning, it helps to see the whole apparatus. Everything in Figure 5 is read from /x and k.php: ways the implant stays on the box, and doors allowing the operator to come back, through a system account or a single web request. Each piece can rebuild/repair all others under a minute, which is why removing any one of them on its own fails. (See Figure 5 below) Figure 5: Persistence channels that rebuild each other, and the backdoors they stay open Detecting It Without IOCs The operator rotates hashes, watermarks, gate values, and hosts between builds, so asking whether a file is known-bad quickly stops working. The better question is who put the file there: compare what is on disk with what the package manager or a clean install says it should be. On the host: triage with beagle.sh PBX admins can run beagle.sh , a report-only script that makes no changes to the host, to check a PBX server for signs of compromise. (See Figure 6 below) Check What it flags Packed shells Several identical, same-size PHP files across unrelated directories Locked files chattr +i or +a under the web root or in hidden directories Unowned .htaccess An .htaccess no installed package accounts for Self-rebuilding cron A cron line that downloads a file and hands it to a shell Accounts An extra UID-0 account, or a full-permission FreePBX admin, nobody created Blocklist Addresses dropped in and out by iptables outside fail2ban's chains Figure 6: beagle.sh (Source: 0x1da5 GitHub ) The script separated one infected server from one clean server of the same FreePBX version, a sample of one, so expect some legitimate findings. However, it cannot tell you whether the credentials have already been left: that happens during the first cron run, within a minute of infection, and long before anyone scans. The upload leaves no file behind, and the takeover script wipes what might have recorded it: the web server, Asterisk, cron and audit logs, plus shell and MySQL histories, which makes forensic timelines hard to reconstruct. With telemetry The most distinctive actions leave little on disk; in our detonation, backdoor accounts were created and deleted 27 seconds apart. These eleven behaviors are detection strategies to build into your own tooling: Layer Behavior What it catches Host crond spawns a shell that downloads a file and runs it The takeover script on its single run, before persistence and before credentials leave Host The web server account spawns a shell The webshell's command box in use Host A cron child rewrites the crontab every minute without reading it first Beacon reinstallation Host chattr +i or touch -r on a file in the web root The lock and the borrowed timestamp Host Twelve PHP files were written to the web root in the same second The webshell copies, as they are written; fan-out Network The PBX contacts staging host roughly every 60 seconds The beacon's rhythm, whatever the address Network Many configuration files read, then outbound POST requests Credentials leaving Web A request with leading encoded whitespace returns 200 for a path not on disk The .htaccess door Decoy Any read of a decoy config file that the implant reads, but nothing legitimate does Credential collection, with no false positives by design Phone Channels originate over AMI or the CLI outside your dial plan A call asking for nothing legitimate Phone CDRs with premium destinations, off-hours calling and unusual concurrency The fraud itself The last two catch the fraud rather than the machinery, whatever the files are called, and whether you ever find the shell. The host rows need process telemetry that PBX appliances rarely have, which is part of why so many stay infected. Why Cleanup Fails, and the Order That Works First move Why it fails on its own Delete the webshell Cron re-runs k.php within minutes and rewrites all 12 copies, the .htaccess, and the immutable flags. Patch FreePBX Sangoma's advisory for CVE-2025-57819 states the fix prevents new exploitation but does not clean a compromised system. Change the admin password The gate and the forged session never use it, and the backdoor accounts bypass the FreePBX login. Shadowserver data showed more than 900 compromised FreePBX instances in February 2026; over 700 of them were still compromised in May. Rebuilding from a clean image is the most reliable fix; if you clean in place, work from the system layer up, because it replants everything above it. Preserve first The takeover script truncates logs, then deletes them, and clears shell and database history, so evidence shrinks with every run: Cut the host off from the internet, or at least block all outbound traffic except to your SIP carrier. Blocking only the two known staging hosts is not enough if the operator has moved. With no route out, the minute-by-minute downloads fail, and nothing more is uploaded. One local loop survives: a watchdog cron line re-runs the cached copy of k.php at /var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2 every minute, rebuilding the webshells offline, which is why cron comes first in the cleanup below. Capture all crontabs and the eight backups listed below, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, shell profiles, and the web root with lsattr output and change times. Export the FreePBX ampusers table, the call records database, and the Asterisk full log, and ask your carrier to preserve CDRs and registration logs. Then clean, in this order Cron and its spares. Clear root's crontab in one go, so the restore and watchdog lines are removed. Then kill any running zen2, devnull2, or serv processes; killed earlier, the watchdog restarts them within a minute. Remove the k.php beacons (/var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2, devnull2, zen222, devnull312, devnull212, /tmp/.cache/update, /dev/shm/.systemd/kernel). Unlock (chattr -i, -a) and delete the eight crontab backups: /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache, /usr/share/.fonts/.config, /var/lib/.dbus/.data, /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority, /opt/.local/.bashrc, /var/cache/.fontconfig/.cfg, /etc/.ssl/.cert, and /root/.config/.pref. Login and boot triggers. Remove the base64 stager from /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, and /etc/rc.local. Accounts and SSH. Remove every extra UID-0 account and any account whose /etc/shadow hash begins with $1$nRz1Cbtk$ (legitimate service accounts with that hash need new passwords, not deletion). Restore sshd_config, where root login was re-enabled. Web application. Remove the 12 webshell copies, the .htaccess, the freepbxusers row in ampusers, and /var/www/html/admin/modules/freepbx_ha/license.php. Credentials. Only now rotate the secrets in the 17 files and across every account on the host. Conclusion The hard part of the campaign used to be getting the implant off the box, and that has not changed. What has changed is that the box is no longer the whole problem: an organization that rebuilds but does not rotate has removed the operator's calling platform and handed over its carrier account. The code ties this generation to the actor in our May report through the takeover script, backdoor hash, and staging host, and a gate rotated in step across JOMANGY and ZenharR. The operator is now rotating exactly the strings defenders were given, so detections built on provenance and behavior will outlast this build, and detections built on its hashes will not. CRIL continues to monitor INJ3CTOR3's infrastructure. Indicators of Compromise Hashes and strings rotate between builds; use them to confirm a finding, not as your only detection. In April, all of these pointed to 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. We assess that the operator replaced the address in plain text and never re-encoded the base64 strings; the credential upload, which names both hosts, appears deliberate. This host is distinct from the scanner 160[.]119[.]76[.]250, which is named in our May report.

Defend: block both hosts in both directions, and decode every base64-encoded string in a crontab or shell profile before deciding which hosts a host talks to. A plain-text review would miss every channel that still reaches 45[.]95[.]147[.]178.

The Webshell: Same Program, New Identifiers

Decoded, the September JOMANGY panel is identical to April's except for the values defenders were told to look for.

Per-build watermark. Our May report advised hunting for trace_e1ebf9066a951be519a24140711839ea, present in every April copy. The September builds carry trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 (45[.]95[.]147[.]178) and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e (160[.]119[.]69[.]4), so that hunt now misses current infections.

One gate for two generations. JOMANGY and ZenharR share a single hardcoded MD5 gate hash, rotated together from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a. Our May report listed the April value under ZenharR only.

A forged administrator session. Behind the gate, the FreePBX button builds an admin session using FreePBX's own ampuser class and setAdmin(); in our lab, it opened the full console without any password. Therefore, changing the FreePBX admin password affects neither the gate nor this session. (See Figure 3 below)

Figure 3: The panel's Freepbx and Elastix buttons forge an admin session without a password

Because each of these identifiers changes between builds, the detection approach later in this report focuses on who put a file on disk rather than on what the file contains.

The .htaccess Door and the Access-Log Gap

k.php writes a seven-line .htaccess to /var/www/html/admin/views/. It does not hide the webshell; it unblocks it, and it lets requests reach a copy without naming it.

RewriteEngine On
# enable symbolic links
Options +FollowSymLinks
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-l
RewriteRule ^\s+ config.php [L]

Request path Status What answered /dir/zzz 404 Nothing /dir/%20zzz, /dir/%09zzz (space, tab, etc) 200 config.php /dir/+zzz 404 Nothing

Simulating an operator and a victim in an isolated environment, we confirmed that a request to a URL containing an encoded space returned a working webshell for the attacker. The access log records only the requested path, never the file that answered, so searching logs for the webshell by its filename can return nothing on a host that is serving it.

Defend: check every .htaccess across the web root for who put it there; one that no package, FreePBX module, or member of your team accounts for is suspect, whatever it contains. Because the takeover script wipes logs, treat log hunting as secondary: requests with %20, %09, or %0A directly after a slash that return 200 are worth a look where logs survive.

What the FreePBX Console Won't Show You

FreePBX lists the trunks it created from its own database; Asterisk reads whatever is in its configuration files. In our lab, a trunk we wrote directly into /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf carried a call while the FreePBX Trunks page reported no records (See Figure 4 below). We did not see the campaign plant one, but its root-equivalent accounts and stolen trunk secrets give the operator everything needed to do so.

Figure 4: Our lab trunk, known to Asterisk and carrying calls, invisible in the FreePBX console

Defend: audit from the Asterisk CLI (pjsip show endpoints, pjsip show registrations, sip show peers, sip show registry) and compare with what the console lists. Review the *_custom.conf files for trunks or contexts that nobody on your team added.

What Keeps It There

Before detecting or cleaning, it helps to see the whole apparatus. Everything in Figure 5 is read from /x and k.php: ways the implant stays on the box, and doors allowing the operator to come back, through a system account or a single web request. Each piece can rebuild/repair all others under a minute, which is why removing any one of them on its own fails. (See Figure 5 below)

Figure 5: Persistence channels that rebuild each other, and the backdoors they stay open

Detecting It Without IOCs

The operator rotates hashes, watermarks, gate values, and hosts between builds, so asking whether a file is known-bad quickly stops working. The better question is who put the file there: compare what is on disk with what the package manager or a clean install says it should be.

On the host: triage with beagle.sh

PBX admins can run beagle.sh, a report-only script that makes no changes to the host, to check a PBX server for signs of compromise. (See Figure 6 below)

Check What it flags Packed shells Several identical, same-size PHP files across unrelated directories Locked files chattr +i or +a under the web root or in hidden directories Unowned .htaccess An .htaccess no installed package accounts for Self-rebuilding cron A cron line that downloads a file and hands it to a shell Accounts An extra UID-0 account, or a full-permission FreePBX admin, nobody created Blocklist Addresses dropped in and out by iptables outside fail2ban's chains

Figure 6: beagle.sh (Source: 0x1da5 GitHub)

The script separated one infected server from one clean server of the same FreePBX version, a sample of one, so expect some legitimate findings. However, it cannot tell you whether the credentials have already been left: that happens during the first cron run, within a minute of infection, and long before anyone scans. The upload leaves no file behind, and the takeover script wipes what might have recorded it: the web server, Asterisk, cron and audit logs, plus shell and MySQL histories, which makes forensic timelines hard to reconstruct.

With telemetry

The most distinctive actions leave little on disk; in our detonation, backdoor accounts were created and deleted 27 seconds apart. These eleven behaviors are detection strategies to build into your own tooling:

Layer Behavior What it catches Host crond spawns a shell that downloads a file and runs it The takeover script on its single run, before persistence and before credentials leave Host The web server account spawns a shell The webshell's command box in use Host A cron child rewrites the crontab every minute without reading it first Beacon reinstallation Host chattr +i or touch -r on a file in the web root The lock and the borrowed timestamp Host Twelve PHP files were written to the web root in the same second The webshell copies, as they are written; fan-out Network The PBX contacts staging host roughly every 60 seconds The beacon's rhythm, whatever the address Network Many configuration files read, then outbound POST requests Credentials leaving Web A request with leading encoded whitespace returns 200 for a path not on disk The .htaccess door Decoy Any read of a decoy config file that the implant reads, but nothing legitimate does Credential collection, with no false positives by design Phone Channels originate over AMI or the CLI outside your dial plan A call asking for nothing legitimate Phone CDRs with premium destinations, off-hours calling and unusual concurrency The fraud itself

The last two catch the fraud rather than the machinery, whatever the files are called, and whether you ever find the shell. The host rows need process telemetry that PBX appliances rarely have, which is part of why so many stay infected.

Why Cleanup Fails, and the Order That Works

First move Why it fails on its own Delete the webshell Cron re-runs k.php within minutes and rewrites all 12 copies, the .htaccess, and the immutable flags. Patch FreePBX Sangoma's advisory for CVE-2025-57819 states the fix prevents new exploitation but does not clean a compromised system. Change the admin password The gate and the forged session never use it, and the backdoor accounts bypass the FreePBX login.

Shadowserver data showed more than 900 compromised FreePBX instances in February 2026; over 700 of them were still compromised in May. Rebuilding from a clean image is the most reliable fix; if you clean in place, work from the system layer up, because it replants everything above it.

Preserve first

The takeover script truncates logs, then deletes them, and clears shell and database history, so evidence shrinks with every run:

  1. Cut the host off from the internet, or at least block all outbound traffic except to your SIP carrier. Blocking only the two known staging hosts is not enough if the operator has moved. With no route out, the minute-by-minute downloads fail, and nothing more is uploaded. One local loop survives: a watchdog cron line re-runs the cached copy of k.php at /var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2 every minute, rebuilding the webshells offline, which is why cron comes first in the cleanup below.

  2. Capture all crontabs and the eight backups listed below, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, shell profiles, and the web root with lsattr output and change times.

  3. Export the FreePBX ampusers table, the call records database, and the Asterisk full log, and ask your carrier to preserve CDRs and registration logs.

Then clean, in this order

  1. Cron and its spares. Clear root's crontab in one go, so the restore and watchdog lines are removed. Then kill any running zen2, devnull2, or serv processes; killed earlier, the watchdog restarts them within a minute. Remove the k.php beacons (/var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2, devnull2, zen222, devnull312, devnull212, /tmp/.cache/update, /dev/shm/.systemd/kernel). Unlock (chattr -i, -a) and delete the eight crontab backups: /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache, /usr/share/.fonts/.config, /var/lib/.dbus/.data, /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority, /opt/.local/.bashrc, /var/cache/.fontconfig/.cfg, /etc/.ssl/.cert, and /root/.config/.pref.

  2. Login and boot triggers. Remove the base64 stager from /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, and /etc/rc.local.

  3. Accounts and SSH. Remove every extra UID-0 account and any account whose /etc/shadow hash begins with $1$nRz1Cbtk$ (legitimate service accounts with that hash need new passwords, not deletion). Restore sshd_config, where root login was re-enabled.

  4. Web application. Remove the 12 webshell copies, the .htaccess, the freepbxusers row in ampusers, and /var/www/html/admin/modules/freepbx_ha/license.php.

  5. Credentials. Only now rotate the secrets in the 17 files and across every account on the host.

Conclusion

The hard part of the campaign used to be getting the implant off the box, and that has not changed. What has changed is that the box is no longer the whole problem: an organization that rebuilds but does not rotate has removed the operator's calling platform and handed over its carrier account.

The code ties this generation to the actor in our May report through the takeover script, backdoor hash, and staging host, and a gate rotated in step across JOMANGY and ZenharR.

The operator is now rotating exactly the strings defenders were given, so detections built on provenance and behavior will outlast this build, and detections built on its hashes will not. CRIL continues to monitor INJ3CTOR3's infrastructure.

Indicators of Compromise

Hashes and strings rotate between builds; use them to confirm a finding, not as your only detection.

Value Type Context 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 IPv4 Staging host since April 160[.]119[.]69[.]4 IPv4 Second staging host and credential collector, new hxxp://45[.]95[.]147[.]178/hima_data/index.php URL Credential upload endpoint hxxp://160[.]119[.]69[.]4/hima_data/index.php URL Credential upload endpoint c6e64453ea8bc0856333b6f57567c9efd8c440410787cae135d1c4a248c07c0d SHA256 /x takeover script, identical on both hosts 38edbfc4ac89619d2bdb3f4bb2626deaaf422868d6d7af640f59d7959903f838 SHA256 k.php, 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 1c14a761620691a43b1a554a9eccd38d21c15d59463945250d4f57b10d20fce9 SHA256 k.php, 160[.]119[.]69[.]4 b54a8d9e98ff36dfe63b2aea97a2003b670f7311595bb4dd072850fed5900a0b SHA256 wr.php, 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 aa6dfd7ee90d9aea5af29ae39c14ff70cf8687118abadd7aa4fc98923f01ffd1 SHA256 wr.php, 160[.]119[.]69[.]4 adeb015fdb37814edc3ed45230f48d2b0e87bb195a5a7e4487c01549b47c744c SHA256 JOMANGY webshell on disk, 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 build d345671e688ee807e1bb9b6fc45e6bb0611bbb1331c33888c8030ec2db47e672 SHA256 JOMANGY webshell on disk, 160[.]119[.]69[.]4 build trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05, trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e String JOMANGY watermarks, one per build 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a MD5 Webshell gate hash, JOMANGY and ZenharR $1$nRz1Cbtk$ Hash prefix Password hash set on backdoor and service accounts

items.title: Microsoft Whistleblower Alleges Foreign Engineer Was Approved to Access U.S. Government Cloud Logs
items.summary: A claimed Microsoft whistleblower has raised concerns about government cloud security after screenshots appeared to show approval for an engineer, allegedly based in India, to receive logs from a U.S. government cloud environment through Microsoft’s escort process. The documents raise questions about access controls but do not establish unauthorized access or a breach. The allegations, shared by Conspiracookie on X, identify Microsoft engineer Viraj Chokhany as the requester. The account says an unnamed whistleblower supplied the images and alleges that Chokhany is not a U.S. citizen. This article has not independently verified either his citizenship or the screenshots’ authenticity. One screenshot shows an internal “SPO Environments” page listing DProdMgd151 under “GCC-Moderate,” with the nickname “GCCM.” The same table lists Department of Defense infrastructure separately. This distinction matters because the supplied evidence concerns a government cloud environment, not a demonstrated connection to classified military systems. BREAKING (EXCLUSIVE): National Security Concerns Leaked by MSFT Whistleblower Leaked Microsoft screenshots show an India-based engineer received approval to view U.S. government cloud logs. A Microsoft whistleblower contacted me and shared screenshots supporting allegations… pic.twitter.com/Ug3k8LYqRI — Conspiracookie (@Conspiracookie) October 27, 2026 Another screenshot shows incident 815678445, titled “Escort Request: GCCM- Request to view GCC-M logs.” It names Chokhany as the creator, lists the O365 Escort Team as the owning team, and marks the request resolved. A discussion entry includes an approval image for his account alias. Approval alone does not prove what information was ultimately disclosed. A further image shows a request to share Geneva logs for two incidents. The visible query links reference environment “dprodmgd151” and SharePoint job definitions. Instructions ask the recipient to load all rows, expand them to display full logs, and share the results. The supplied screenshots show no returned log contents. What Microsoft’s GCC Rules Require Microsoft’s published GCC service description says staff have no standing access to customer content. Employees seeking temporary elevated permissions that would expose such content must first pass screening, including verification of U.S. citizenship, criminal history checks, and other background reviews. However, the same document says GCC customer support carries no general assurance about an agent’s physical location or citizenship. It warns customers not to share sensitive information until confirming the recipient’s authorization. That distinction makes the contents of the requested logs central to assessing whether protected customer information crossed an access boundary. The screenshots do not establish whether the requested logs contained customer content covered by those citizenship checks. They also do not identify the affected government customer or show a completed transfer. The whistleblower’s suggested FedRAMP violation therefore remains an allegation, not a verified compliance finding. Under the digital escort model described by ProPublica , authorized U.S. personnel carry out work directed by overseas engineers. Its investigation found that some escorts lacked the technical skills needed to supervise engineers with greater expertise, weakening the intended oversight. The supplied ticket guidance adds context. It states, “ESCORTS ARE NOT ENGINEERS,” and expects requesters to provide the information needed to complete their tasks. It also says escorts will execute commands exactly as written in the ticket and are not permitted to troubleshoot issues. These instructions deserve examination, but do not independently prove misconduct. Cyber Security News previously covered reports about Microsoft’s China-based SharePoint support engineers . That reporting provides background on overseas support arrangements, not evidence that the engineer identified in these screenshots acted improperly. In August 2025, the Pentagon called Microsoft’s use of China-based engineers a “breach of trust” and required an outside audit. Microsoft had announced an end to its support for Defense Department cloud systems. Those developments concerned a separate arrangement. Separately, SharePoint zero-day attacks show why government security attracts scrutiny. This allegation, however, requires evidence about the actual logs shared, approval scope, and safeguards before any breach or rule violation can be established. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Critical UEFI Firmware Flaw Could Expose Millions of Servers to Pre-Boot Code Execution
items.summary: A critical bug in open-source EDK II firmware lets a remote attacker run code on a machine before the operating system starts. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-97631. It sits in the network boot (PXE) driver and received a CVSS v4 score of 9.5. The advisory lists the NetworkPkg package in EDK II master as of September 14, 2026. EDK II is the reference code that many firmware makers use to build UEFI firmware, so the bug can reach servers, desktops, and laptops that boot over a network. UEFI Vulnerability With No Patch The advisory page still says “Not patched currently,” yet a fix has already been merged into the public code. Vendors must now ship that fix in their own firmware updates, which usually takes much longer. During a PXE boot, the driver named UefiPxeBcDxe listens for ICMP error messages from the network. It copies each message into a fixed 504-byte field. The copy code checks sizes poorly in both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers. For a message longer than 504 bytes, it keeps copying anyway. It also moves the write position forward by the total length so far instead of the length of the current piece. Attacker-controlled bytes therefore land past the end of the field. Nothing earlier on the receive path limits the message size. The attacker needs no login and no user action. They only have to send one ICMP error message addressed to the client’s IP address while it is PXE booting. The message can come from any distance on the network. The window of exposure lasts as long as the PXE boot does. The damage comes in two forms. The simple one is a crash. The next ICMP error triggers a CPU exception inside the DXE core, and the boot hangs. That blocks OS installs and recovery. The worse form needs more knowledge. An attacker who knows the exact firmware build can plant a fake event in the same packet. The firmware then runs the attacker’s bytes at the highest privilege level, before Secure Boot or measured boot checks anything. Servers face the most risk because data centers often rely on PXE to install and rebuild machines in bulk. Tools that run on every reprovisioning cycle give attackers repeated chances to strike. UEFI Security Flaws The discovery adds to a series of firmware security failures involving network boot code, trusted signing keys, and even the images shown when a computer starts. These flaws have different entry points, but they share a concern: attackers can target code that runs before normal operating system defenses take control. One example is PKfail, a firmware supply-chain problem caused by device makers shipping products with test Platform Keys that should never have been trusted in production. These keys help control the Secure Boot trust chain. An attacker who obtains the matching private key can use it to replace trusted boot settings and allow malicious software to run despite Secure Boot being enabled. Cyber Security News previously covered how PKfail affected more than 200 device models , while CERT/CC’s advisory explains the risk of persistent malware on affected systems. Another example, LogoFAIL, exposed weaknesses in the code that reads manufacturer logo images during startup. A specially crafted image could trigger code execution during the Driver Execution Environment, or DXE, phase. This is the same early firmware stage targeted by the newly disclosed PXE flaw, although the delivery method is different. As detailed in Cyber Security News’ LogoFAIL coverage , the bugs affected image-reading code used across several firmware vendors. PixieFail provides an even closer comparison. Disclosed in January 2024, it involved nine flaws in the IPv6 network stack of TianoCore EDK II. Those weaknesses affected network boot operations used in data centers and enterprise environments. The fix is pull request 13302 . It adds proper boundary checks and corrects the pointer math. Oversized ICMP messages are now cut short once the buffer is full. The patch also clears the buffer before each copy, so stale bytes from an earlier error cannot remain. It adds unit tests that failed before the change and pass after it. Maintainers merged it on October 15, 2026. The merge was public days before the advisory appeared on October 22. A maintainer later admitted that the embargo was broken by mistake and that the pull request was opened in the open. He asked reporters to keep using private GitHub advisories for coordinated disclosure. He also said a backlog of reports exists. The advisory credits Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes-Mitra of Google for finding the bug and proposing the fix. Ask your server and firmware vendors when they will ship an update with this fix. Until then, limit exposure by keeping PXE boot traffic on isolated provisioning networks. Block unexpected ICMP error messages aimed at booting machines, and turn off PXE on systems that do not need it. Teams should also review the CISA and NSA Secure Boot guidance for wider hardening steps. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

One example is PKfail, a firmware supply-chain problem caused by device makers shipping products with test Platform Keys that should never have been trusted in production. These keys help control the Secure Boot trust chain.

An attacker who obtains the matching private key can use it to replace trusted boot settings and allow malicious software to run despite Secure Boot being enabled. Cyber Security News previously covered how PKfail affected more than 200 device models, while CERT/CC’s advisory explains the risk of persistent malware on affected systems.

Another example, LogoFAIL, exposed weaknesses in the code that reads manufacturer logo images during startup. A specially crafted image could trigger code execution during the Driver Execution Environment, or DXE, phase. This is the same early firmware stage targeted by the newly disclosed PXE flaw, although the delivery method is different. As detailed in Cyber Security News’ LogoFAIL coverage, the bugs affected image-reading code used across several firmware vendors.

PixieFail provides an even closer comparison. Disclosed in January 2024, it involved nine flaws in the IPv6 network stack of TianoCore EDK II. Those weaknesses affected network boot operations used in data centers and enterprise environments.

The fix is pull request 13302. It adds proper boundary checks and corrects the pointer math. Oversized ICMP messages are now cut short once the buffer is full. The patch also clears the buffer before each copy, so stale bytes from an earlier error cannot remain. It adds unit tests that failed before the change and pass after it. Maintainers merged it on October 15, 2026.

The merge was public days before the advisory appeared on October 22. A maintainer later admitted that the embargo was broken by mistake and that the pull request was opened in the open. He asked reporters to keep using private GitHub advisories for coordinated disclosure. He also said a backlog of reports exists. The advisory credits Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes-Mitra of Google for finding the bug and proposing the fix.

Ask your server and firmware vendors when they will ship an update with this fix. Until then, limit exposure by keeping PXE boot traffic on isolated provisioning networks. Block unexpected ICMP error messages aimed at booting machines, and turn off PXE on systems that do not need it. Teams should also review the CISA and NSA Secure Boot guidance for wider hardening steps.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Discord to Make Discoverable Public Server Messages Searchable on Google
items.summary: Discord will make selected messages from Discoverable Servers searchable through Google and other search engines, opening some community discussions to the wider web. Announced on October 27, the change begins on November 16, 2026, with Server Web Pages and discussion summaries. Individual messages will start rolling out in mid-December, not November, giving users and moderators time to review their privacy settings before posts become searchable. According to Discord’s announcement , the aim is to make useful answers easier to find without first searching inside Discord. The company says knowledge shared in gaming guides, support discussions, and community forums often remains difficult for outsiders to reach. Which Discord Messages Will Appear on Google? The update applies only to Discoverable Servers, which anyone can find and join without an invitation. These communities must have at least 1,000 members, be eight weeks old, and meet activity and safety rules. Discord says more than 63,000 servers currently fall into this category. Private servers, direct messages, and group direct messages are excluded. Every Discoverable Server will have a Server Web Page from November 16. Where moderators have not published one, Discord will create a default page using the Server Profile. Automated Channel Summaries may appear that day, covering discussions from November 16 onward. Individual Channel Messages follow in mid-December through a gradual rollout. Only eligible messages sent from that point onward can appear. Older message histories will not be published through this feature. Usernames and avatars will be hidden, while messages will initially appear as text. Discord’s member guidance says participating channels will display an icon and a notice before users post. Public threads and forums can qualify, but private threads and private forums remain excluded. How Users Can Stop Their Messages Appearing Users can open User Settings > Data & Privacy and disable “Show my message content from Discoverable channels on web pages.” This account-wide switch covers every Discoverable Server they belong to. Discord says the control can be changed through its desktop app or browser and applies across devices, including mobile. The setting is enabled by default in most regions. It is disabled by default in the EU/EEA, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea. Teen accounts are excluded and cannot enable the feature. Server and channel eligibility rules still apply even where a user’s setting is enabled. Turning the switch off only protects messages sent afterward. Messages posted while it was enabled can still appear, even if they have not reached a web page yet. Users must delete those messages to remove them from Discord’s pages. Search engines may retain indexed or cached copies longer and require separate removal steps. These controls address a planned publishing feature, not a security breach. That distinction separates this announcement from the earlier Discord customer support data breach , which involved unauthorized access through a third-party provider. Moderators can manage participation through Server Settings > Web Presence. They can exclude selected channels or disable all channel participation. Without changes, public channels remain enabled. User opt-outs do not disable Channel Summaries, which have separate admin controls. Communities unwilling to maintain a Server Web Page can leave Discovery and remain Community Servers. For security teams, the key concern is wider exposure rather than a newly disclosed flaw. Removing usernames does not remove identifying details written inside messages. Public support channels therefore deserve review before publication, particularly where members discuss workplace systems or share personal information. Search visibility also should not be mistaken for proof of trust. Earlier reporting on expired Discord invite links used to spread malware showed attackers directing visitors into fake communities. Readers finding Discord answers through Google should check destinations and avoid running commands presented as account verification steps. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.summary_html:
Welcome to volume forty-seven of Scrolls, a newsletter for sharing cool stuff from the IndieWeb, Fediverse & Cybersecurity realms.

You might be thinking, “Woah! Scrolls is back? Where’s this guy been for the last 3 and a half months??” A fair question to be sure. I’m very much still alive — just… my life has required my energy to be allocated elsewhere. I’ve still been going through my feeds with some regularity and reading and saving the cool stuff I find. So I’ve got a bit of a backlog of things to publish and share. There’s a decent chance you’ll see a burst of Scrolls issues over the next few weeks or so. I don’t have much of a concrete plan with this longer term though. I’d like to get to 50 issues, and then assess. What’s the best, and most sustainable way for me to continue to share things I find with everyone who has taken the time to subscribe to the feed or to the larger blog itself. Maybe it’s just more of the same. Maybe I move to more of a once-a-month cadence. Maybe I take it in a wildly different creative direction. Not sure! But there’s more to come, one way or another. If you’re reading this, thanks for staying with me. Now, onto the cool stuff!

IndieWeb

You should have a personal website (Yep! Me saying this again). Not because what you have to say matters in the grand scheme of the universe, but because what you say or put on your site can matter to someone, even if that’s just one person, even if that someone is only you. But in my opinion, there’s a ton of reasons to start a personal website. Even if it’s just for silly things.

A lot of people like to wax poetic about the web of yore, but there’s no reason that the web we so fondly remember has to be a thing of the past. There’s still so much out there that remains interesting, whimsical, creative and human. You only need to know where to look.

So go build a site and do some cool, fun, creative stuff with it. Here’s some ideas! Make a shuffle button, build a website for someone else, make an 88x31 button or create a comment section. One thing you can steer clear from though… using AI images. Yuck.

Fediverse

The Fediverse might be messy, but it’s really the only good choice right now.

Cybersecurity

Well, hello! 👋

Here’s some cyber stuff. Y’know, back in the days before “4” and PHP chaos 😭

I’ve gotcha a guide on Yubikeys, a history on the web’s trust model, a warning about trusted publishing, the “Coding Agent Attack Matrix” and some sage advice about the “vulnpocalypse”.

Thanks for reading Scrolls!
